relatedGuides.text: What Does “Processed Locally in Your Browser” Mean?

title: What Does “Processed Locally in Your Browser” Mean?

body.content: Local processing means the browser on your device reads and transforms a selected file instead of first sending it to a remote processing server. The website can still download the code needed for that work and make ordinary website requests. Local file processing describes where the operation happens; it does not mean the whole website is disconnected from the internet.

body.caption: Where the work happens
head: Question
Local processing
Server processing
rows: Who reads and transforms the file?
Software on a remote server after an upload.
Primarily the server’s processor and memory.
The page and any uncached code, models, or other requests.
Uploading the input, processing requests, and receiving the result.
Actual upload behavior, other requests, and local storage.
Upload handling, retention, access, and deletion policies.

body.content: For example, rotating a PDF locally lets your browser create the rotated copy from the selected original. A server-based service receives the PDF, creates a copy remotely, and sends the result back. Either approach can have additional features; the label alone does not describe every data flow.

body.text: What happens when you select a file?

body.content: A browser file picker gives the page access to the files you choose. Selection and upload are separate actions: JavaScript can read the selected bytes locally, but a website can also send those bytes over the network. A button labeled “Choose file” does not establish which behavior follows.

Processing may hold input bytes, decoded images, page previews, and output bytes in memory at the same time. A temporary object URL, usually starting with blob:, lets the page display or download browser-held data. Creating that URL is not an upload or a public sharing link. Releasing it lets the browser reclaim associated resources; it is not a promise of secure erasure from device memory or storage.

body.text: Why does a local tool still download things or use memory?

body.content: JavaScript runs application logic. WebAssembly lets browsers run compiled processing engines, while browser features can decode images and draw previews. None of these technologies automatically prevents a website from making network requests.

A tool may need to download a reusable OCR language file or a background-removal model before it can work. Receiving that shared resource is different from sending your document to a server. The processing itself still consumes CPU and RAM: a compressed photo can expand into a much larger pixel buffer, and a long PDF may need many page previews. Large jobs can be slow or exceed a phone’s available memory.

body.text: What does “offline after first load” depend on?

body.content: Offline use depends on the exact page, processing engine, and required resources being available in the browser cache. Opening a homepage once does not necessarily cache every tool. Browsers may clear cached data, private browsing may retain less, and a different language or model may need a fresh download. Test the specific workflow offline before depending on it.

body.text: What local processing does not guarantee

items: It does not prove that a site has no analytics, cookies, contact services, or other network traffic.
It does not remove metadata or visible personal information from the output.
It does not protect a downloaded file from other people or software with access to your device.
It does not eliminate risks from browser extensions, compromised code, or an insecure device.

content: Check a service’s current privacy disclosures and the behavior of the particular tool. If you plan to share the result, also review

title: PDF Compression: File Size vs Quality Explained

body.content: PDF compression can reduce file size without changing the visible page, or it can trade image detail for fewer bytes. The result depends on what occupies the file and which compression methods are used. There is no single quality setting that suits every PDF: keep the original and judge the smaller copy against its intended use.

body.text: Why are some PDFs so large?

body.content: A PDF can contain text, vector drawings, raster images, embedded fonts, and other document data. A short brochure with large photographs can outweigh a long text-only report. Scanned pages often store the entire page—including the letters—as pixels, whereas native text and vector lines can stay sharp without a full-page image.

content: This distinction explains why a blurrier compressed scan may also have blurrier text. See
for the difference between page images and a text layer.

body.content: Structural compression rewrites or packs PDF data more efficiently. Image compression may reduce pixel dimensions or encode images with stronger lossy settings. Other products may remove document features or rebuild pages as images. These methods have different consequences; “compress PDF” does not identify one universal process.

Resolution describes how many image pixels cover a physical area, often discussed as DPI in PDF settings. For example, an image 1,200 pixels wide placed across six inches provides 200 pixels per inch. Reducing its pixel dimensions removes detail. Enlarging it afterward cannot restore the missing information.

JPEG-style lossy encoding also discards information. Stronger settings can produce block patterns, halos around letters, or smeared texture even when pixel dimensions stay the same. Small labels and scanned fine print often expose these changes before a large photograph does.

body.text: Choose quality for the actual destination

body.caption: Priorities for a compressed copy
head: Goal
Recommended priority
What to inspect
rows: Meet the limit while keeping the content usable.
Small text, stamps, and images after downloading.
Normal reading size and zoomed diagrams.
Fine text, photographs, lines, and a sample printed page.
Keep the original rather than replacing it with a compressed derivative.

body.content: If a form requires a smaller attachment, start with moderate compression and increase only as needed. A document that meets the byte limit but makes an identification number unreadable has failed the practical task. Keep an unmodified master separately so you can make a different copy later.

body.text: Why did the file barely shrink?

body.content: Already compressed images and efficiently stored text leave less redundant data to remove. Embedded resources or protected document features can also limit safe changes. Recompressing an existing small PDF does not guarantee further savings; a new encoding may even be larger. A dramatic reduction on one scanned brochure does not predict the result for another file.

body.text: What the current SoraFiles compressor does

content: uses a strength control and an optional maximum file size. It first attempts a structural reduction. Additional image compression skips protected content, and for documents with detected native text a smaller result is kept only when every page still has the same text. The checks compare candidate pages and keep an accepted smaller result. Signed documents are returned unchanged.

body.content: The tool may return the original when a candidate is not smaller or does not pass its checks. Those checks reduce the risk of a bad result, but they are not a guarantee of identical appearance or preservation of every PDF feature. SoraFiles’ current behavior should not be assumed to describe another compressor.

Check links, forms, and other features you need. For printing, inspect a printed sample.
Compare the actual file size with the destination’s limit, then keep both the original and the accepted copy.

title: Why Does PDF to Word Formatting Change?

body.content: PDF-to-Word formatting changes because a PDF describes a fixed visual page, while a Word document describes editable content that can flow and be laid out again. A converter often has to infer paragraphs, columns, and tables from positioned text. The PDF may not contain enough information to recreate the original document’s structure.

body.text: Why a page that looks right can convert badly

body.content: In a PDF, separate pieces of text can be drawn at specific coordinates. A human sees one paragraph or two columns, but the stored operations do not necessarily identify that relationship. WordprocessingML, the document format inside DOCX, represents structures such as paragraphs, text runs, and tables. Converting between these models involves interpretation.

For example, a two-column newsletter may store text fragments in an order that differs from normal reading order. A converter can accidentally join a left-column sentence to a right-column heading. Likewise, numbers aligned to look like a table may have no actual table structure to recover.

body.text: Why do fonts and line breaks change?

body.content: A PDF may embed a font or only a subset of its characters. That does not guarantee the same usable font is available to the converted Word document. Font substitution, character widths, paragraph spacing, and page margins can change line wrapping. A small difference near the beginning can move content onto another page.

body.caption: Two different conversion goals
head: Approach
What you get
Main tradeoff
rows: A rendered image of each PDF page placed in a DOCX.
The page can look similar, but its text is not ordinary editable Word text.
Recognized or extracted text rebuilt into Word content.
You can edit the text, but layout and document structure may change.

body.content: A page-image document can be useful when a recipient specifically needs a DOCX containing the visual pages. It is usually a poor choice for rewriting paragraphs. Editable reconstruction suits text revisions, provided you allow time to review headings, lists, tables, and reading order. Neither approach recovers the original source file perfectly.

body.text: What changes when the PDF is scanned?

content: An image-only scan has no usable text for a normal text extractor. OCR estimates the characters from pixels. It can misread a zero as the letter O or merge adjacent columns, and recognizing the words does not recover the original styles and document structure. Learn how

content.text: a searchable scan differs from a native PDF

It does not promise reconstruction of the original layout or all graphical content. Visual output puts rendered PDF pages into DOCX as images.

body.content: Choose editable output if changing the wording matters most. Choose visual output if preserving the page’s visible arrangement matters more than editing its text. Check the selected output option before conversion and review a complex page before relying on the whole document.

title: JPG vs PNG vs WebP: Which Image Format Should You Use?

body.content: Choose JPG for ordinary photographs and broad compatibility, PNG when lossless pixel preservation or transparency matters, and WebP for efficient web delivery when the destination accepts it. The best choice depends on the image and its use. No format is always smallest or always best.

body.caption: JPG, PNG, and WebP at a glance
head: Feature
JPG
PNG
WebP
rows: Not in an ordinary JPEG image.
APNG supports animation; ordinary PNG exports may be still images.
Supported by the format; not every exporter retains it.
Useful for web delivery; compare the actual output.
Good for sharp text and exact pixels.
Lossless mode can suit sharp graphics.
Poor fit if transparency is required.
Good when transparency and destination support fit.
Lossless is possible; verify editor support.
Widely accepted by devices and upload forms.
Widely supported, though some forms require JPG.
Supported by modern browsers; older apps and specific forms may reject it.

body.text: Why JPG works well for photographs

body.content: Ordinary JPG encoding discards some information to store a photograph compactly. Smooth changes in color and natural texture can tolerate that tradeoff better than tiny lettering. Strong compression can create visible blocks and edge halos. Repeatedly editing and saving a lossy copy can accumulate damage, so keep an original or lossless working file.

A transparent logo cannot remain transparent in JPG. The conversion must provide a background color, which may differ from the page where you later place it. Check the result against its intended background before sending it.

body.text: When is PNG the better choice?

body.content: PNG preserves the encoded pixel values without lossy image compression and supports alpha transparency. That makes it useful for screenshots, diagrams, line art, and raster logos. A screenshot of small interface text is a concrete case where a slightly larger PNG can be more useful than a JPG with fuzzy letters.

Lossless encoding does not undo earlier damage. Converting a blurred JPG to PNG preserves the already-blurred pixels. PNG also does not preserve an editor’s layers, vectors, or every piece of source metadata just because its image compression is lossless.

WebP offers both lossy and lossless encoding, plus transparency and animation support. It is useful for website images when your publishing system and visitors’ software support it. Actual size and appearance depend on the source, dimensions, and encoding settings; a WebP extension alone does not tell you whether the file is lossless.

For an email attachment or an application form, the recipient’s accepted formats matter more than a theoretical size advantage. If a form requires JPG, use a real JPG export. Renaming photo.webp to photo.jpg changes the filename, not the encoded image.

title: File Metadata: What It Is and What to Check Before Sharing

body.content: File metadata is information stored alongside a file’s main content, such as an author name, capture time, camera model, or document title. The fields vary by format and by the software that created the file. Not every file contains sensitive metadata, but checking it can prevent sharing details you did not intend to include.

body.text: What metadata might a file contain?

body.caption: Examples to inspect
head: File type
Possible fields
What to remember
rows: EXIF capture time, camera/device details, orientation, software, and GPS coordinates when recorded.

A PDF can also contain other metadata and document features.
Author, last editor, document properties, company, and custom properties.
Comments and tracked changes are separate things to review.

body.content: For example, a photograph can show an ordinary wall while its location field identifies where it was taken. Conversely, a screenshot may contain little capture metadata but visibly display a name in a notification. The appropriate check depends on the file, not an assumption that all metadata is sensitive.

If information is visibly present, use a suitable redaction workflow and verify the saved result. Covering text with a shape can leave the original text recoverable. Metadata cleanup also does not necessarily remove comments, attachments, hidden document content, or revision history.

Re-exporting a PDF can affect quality, text selection, or document features. Neither operation is a universal substitute for inspection.

title: Scanned PDF vs Searchable PDF: What’s the Difference?

body.content: A scanned PDF often contains pictures of pages rather than selectable text. A searchable PDF contains a text layer that software can search, select, copy, or index. OCR can add recognized text to a scanned PDF while preserving the visible page image, but the recognized words may contain mistakes.

body.text: Image-only, native, and searchable scanned PDFs

body.caption: How the three kinds of PDF differ
head: Feature
Image-only scan
Native digital PDF
OCR/searchable scan
rows: Usually available when text is encoded accessibly.
Available where recognized text was added.
Cannot search the pictured words as text.
Searches the recognized text, including its errors.
Text, vectors, images, or a mixture.
Often the same page image with a hidden text layer.
Yes, to recognize the pictured words.
Usually not for readable native text.
Already performed, though a poor result may need another attempt.
No OCR errors in native text; extraction can still have problems.
Possible even when the visible scan looks correct.

body.content: A PDF can mix these types: a digital report may include a scanned appendix. Try searching for a distinctive visible word and copying a sentence from several pages. A failed search alone is not definitive proof of an image-only scan; text encoding, permissions, or a poor OCR layer can also interfere.

body.text: How does an invisible text layer work?

body.content: OCR—optical character recognition—estimates characters from an image. A PDF exporter can store the recognized words invisibly while leaving the scan visible. Search then uses those stored words, not a fresh reading of the pixels. Good alignment places the hidden words over their matching image locations so selection and highlighting feel natural.

For example, a scan visibly showing invoice number 1080 might have 1O8O in its OCR layer. Searching for the correct number can fail even though the page image is unchanged. Copying the number into a spreadsheet carries the recognition error with it.

items: Low resolution loses character detail; enlarging a blurry scan cannot recover the missing strokes.
Skew, motion blur, shadows, noise, and compression artifacts make letter shapes harder to separate.
An inappropriate recognition language can produce the wrong words or characters.
Handwriting and unusual fonts are less predictable than clear printed text.
Columns, tables, footnotes, and rotated labels can confuse reading order even when individual letters are recognized.

body.content: A searchable PDF is not automatically a well-structured or accessible document. Recognizing words does not necessarily create proper headings, table relationships, reading order, or document tags. OCR also does not recreate the original Word source.

Pages with existing native text are not subject to that added-text encoding in the same way, but they still need a practical search and copy check.
